title: Should you not eat gluten?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain celiac disease as an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten, describing how the small intestine lining is damaged, why it is underdiagnosed (about thirty undiagnosed for every diagnosed case), its symptoms, and the gluten-free diet as the only treatment. They discuss the link to Norman Borlaug's green revolution wheat, the gluten-free fad and its links to autism diets, gluten in unexpected foods, gluten-free beer, and the Catholic Church's ruling that Communion bread must contain wheat. The episode closes with listener mail about a listener's first kiss in Venice and a sinking-boat story request.

segments.title: Opening banter and green revolution setup
segments.summary: The hosts open with small talk about Chuck's fingers and the holidays, then discuss Norman Borlaug, the green revolution wheat breeding, and the environmental downsides of intensive farming.

segments.title: Gluten and celiac disease introduction
segments.summary: The hosts link the green revolution to rising gluten exposure and rising celiac rates, and introduce celiac disease as an autoimmune disorder triggered by a food protein.

segments.title: How celiac disease damages the small intestine
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the small intestine absorbs nutrients and that in celiac disease its lining is damaged, so nutrients pass through, causing malnourishment. They describe the immune system attacking the body's own enzyme that breaks down gluten, and the genetic markers found in sufferers.

segments.title: Symptoms and underdiagnosis
segments.summary: The hosts list symptoms including chronic diarrhea, weight loss, foul-smelling stools, gas, muscle cramps, joint pain, irritability, depression, and a skin rash called dermatitis herpetiformis. They note that about thirty people are undiagnosed for every one diagnosed and that symptoms mimic IBS, Crohn's disease, and cystic fibrosis.

segments.title: Gluten-free diet, fads, and testing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the gluten-free diet as the only treatment, its popularity as a health fad, and the gluten-sensitivity distinction. They advise getting diagnosed before going gluten-free because the diet can distort blood test results.

segments.title: Gluten-free diet and autism
segments.summary: The hosts describe the gluten-free casein-free diet used by some parents of autistic children, based on a theory about peptides acting as opiates, which they say has not been studied enough. They promise a future autism episode.

segments.title: Gluten in foods and gluten-free products
segments.summary: The hosts list foods containing gluten, including baked goods, salad dressing, soy sauce, ice cream, lipstick, toothpaste, beer, and envelope adhesive, and note the growing number of gluten-free products and gluten-free beer.

segments.title: Catholic Church and gluten in communion wafers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Catholic Church's ruling that Eucharist bread must be made with wheat, and the case of a young girl whose first communion with a low-gluten wafer was declared invalid.

segments.title: Closing advice and resources
segments.summary: The hosts recap advice to see a doctor for a gluten sensitivity and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks article by Molly Edmonds on celiac disease.

segments.title: Listener mail: first kiss in Venice
segments.summary: A listener recounts her first kiss with a British man on a dock in Venice and their long-distance relationship, and an update says the couple broke up and he is trying to win her back. The hosts also ask for sinking-boat stories.
